Sorry, pressed send before i meant too. Here’s a quick solution:
pincus = function(A) {
  if (A < 20) {
     return(2)
  } else {
     return 2*((A - 2e-10) %/% 10)
  }
}

B = pincus(A)

The %/% operator does integer division, so that it returns the largest integer multiple of 10 that is less than (A - 2e-10). I subtract 2e-10 from A so this increments B only when A is slightly more than a multiple of 10.

Michael’s right. Here’s a properly vectorized version that doesn’t require sapply, and a test:
pincus = function(A) {
  ifelse(test = A < 20, yes = 2, no = 2*((A - 2e-10) %/% 10))
}
dat = data.frame(A = c(1.56, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 1200))
dat$B = pincus(dat$A)

print(dat)

ifelse is a vectorized version of if() {} else {} so it tests each value. With this, you get:

1     1.56   2
2    10.00   2
3    15.00   2
4    20.00   2
5    30.00   4
6    35.00   6
7    40.00   6
8    45.00   8
9    50.00   8
10 1200.00 238

messages.body_plain:
Hey y'all,

I'm trying to write a for-loop that finds the high tide in a vector of 10-minute tide recordings.  When it finds the high tide, I'd like it to spit that value into a new vector.  I generated some simple sample data (attached) that simulates the dataset with integers.  So far, I have:

d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

m=0

for (i in 1:length(d$numbers)) {

if(d$numbers[i]>=m) {d$numbers[i] -> m}

else {m=m}

}

This successfully spits out the first "high tide" value (8), but I don't know how to make it keep going through the whole vector to get the next two values (which should be 5 and 8, respectively).

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Best,
Myfanwy

--

University of California at Davis
Biotelemetry Lab

Hi Myfanwy,

This is a slightly different logical approach, but it will create a vector of  c( 8, 5, 8) as you suggest:

d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

highs = NA
j=1
for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
  {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
       {highs[j] <- d$numbers[i] ; j = j+1}
  }

However, I wonder if you also don't want a way to extract the row in which the high tides occur? Here is the same code with a few extra lines to pull that information as well and put it all into one dataframe:

d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

highs = data.frame(tide.height = rep(NA,10), tide.row = rep(NA,10))
j=1
for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
  {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
         { highs$tide.height[j] <- d$numbers[i]
           highs$tide.row[j] <- as.numeric(rownames(d)[i])
           j = j+1}
  }
highs = highs[!is.na <http://is.na>(highs$tide.height),]

The 'rep(NA,10)' at the top and the matching line at the bottom to remove extra NAs is a bit messy, plus the value of 10 would potentially have to be increased for larger datasets. If anyone has better code to clean that up, please do!

- Anna

Tim Poisot posted a function for finding peaks in noisy data here: http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/. findpeaks takes a bandwidth (bw=) argument, which is the width of a sliding window in which peaks are calculated. If you set the window to half the period of the tides, you’ll only get one peak per tide. I’ve pasted the function and an example below.
findpeaks <- function(vec,bw=1,x.coo=c(1:length(vec)))
{
  pos.x.max <- NULL
    pos.y.max <- NULL
    pos.x.min <- NULL
    pos.y.min <- NULL

  for(i in 1:(length(vec)-1))     {
    if((i+1+bw)>length(vec)) {
        sup.stop <-  length(vec)}else{sup.stop <- i+1+bw
                }
        if((i-bw)<1){inf.stop <- 1}else{inf.stop <- i-bw}
        subset.sup <- vec[(i+1):sup.stop]
        subset.inf <- vec[inf.stop:(i-1)]

        is.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == 0
        is.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == 0

        no.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == length(subset.inf)
        no.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == length(subset.sup)

        if(is.max & is.nomin){
            pos.x.max <- c(pos.x.max,x.coo[i])
            pos.y.max <- c(pos.y.max,vec[i])
        }
        if(no.max & no.nomin){
            pos.x.min <- c(pos.x.min,x.coo[i])
            pos.y.min <- c(pos.y.min,vec[i])
        }
    }
    return(list(pos.x.max,pos.y.max,pos.x.min,pos.y.min))
}

Example:
x <- sin((1:200)*pi/50) + 2 + rnorm(200, 0, 0.1) # generate some noisy periodic data

fp = findpeaks(x, bw=10) #only count peaks that are the max over a period of 10 points

plot(x, type="l")
points(fp[[1]], fp[[2]], lwd=2, col="red")

Note that fp[[1]] and fp[[2]] are the x and y values at the peaks. fp[[3]] and fp[[4]] are the same for the pits.

> Tim Poisot posted a function for finding peaks in noisy data here: http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/. findpeaks takes a bandwidth (bw=) argument, which is the width of a sliding window in which peaks are calculated. If you set the window to half the period of the tides, you’ll only get one peak per tide. I’ve pasted the function and an example below.
> findpeaks <- function(vec,bw=1,x.coo=c(1:length(vec)))
> {
>   pos.x.max <- NULL
>     pos.y.max <- NULL
>     pos.x.min <- NULL
>     pos.y.min <- NULL
>
>   for(i in 1:(length(vec)-1))     {
>     if((i+1+bw)>length(vec)) {
>         sup.stop <-  length(vec)}else{sup.stop <- i+1+bw
>                 }
>         if((i-bw)<1){inf.stop <- 1}else{inf.stop <- i-bw}
>         subset.sup <- vec[(i+1):sup.stop]
>         subset.inf <- vec[inf.stop:(i-1)]
>
>         is.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == 0
>         is.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == 0
>
>         no.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == length(subset.inf)
>         no.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == length(subset.sup)
>
>         if(is.max & is.nomin){
>             pos.x.max <- c(pos.x.max,x.coo[i])
>             pos.y.max <- c(pos.y.max,vec[i])
>         }
>         if(no.max & no.nomin){
>             pos.x.min <- c(pos.x.min,x.coo[i])
>             pos.y.min <- c(pos.y.min,vec[i])
>         }
>     }
>     return(list(pos.x.max,pos.y.max,pos.x.min,pos.y.min))
> }
>
> Example:
> x <- sin((1:200)*pi/50) + 2 + rnorm(200, 0, 0.1) # generate some noisy periodic data
>
> fp = findpeaks(x, bw=10) #only count peaks that are the max over a period of 10 points
>
> plot(x, type="l")
> points(fp[[1]], fp[[2]], lwd=2, col="red")
>
